name: Desmanthus

project_scope.native_range_status: Each taxon awaits independent 3-county documentation; Texas native at state level is not county PASS
project_scope.first_pass: Five canonical cards, twelve physical photos: three each for acuminatus, illinoensis, leptolobus; one velutinus and two virgatus. Full species-face coverage; not full micro-diagnostic completion.

look_here_first: FIRST find the WHOLE twice-compound (bipinnate) leaf: several featherlike PINNAE radiate along one main leaf axis; each pinna has many tiny paired LEAFLETS. Then inspect the pale puffball flower head and mature PODS. Short, broad, strongly curled pods point to D. illinoensis; long, narrow, mostly straight pods point to D. leptolobus. Check the tiny extrafloral gland above the leaf base and 5 versus 10 stamens with a hand lens only when the part is really visible; photographs of those microstructures are still needed.
shared_traits: Unarmed perennial legumes or subshrubs; some species prostrate, some erect, some wooded at base
Bipinnate leaves: primary leaf with multiple opposite pairs of pinnae, each carrying many tiny opposite leaflets
Often a visible extrafloral gland on the upper rachis between the lowest pair of pinnae; gland position helps separate Neptunia/Mimosa
Small globose or short oval whitish-green flower heads on axillary stalks, often with projecting stamens
Flat beanlike pods, narrow or sickle-shaped, often radiating from base of head; seeds and pods stronger diagnostics than flower color
field_study_sequence: 1 · Confirm Fabaceae and a COMPLETE leaf; inspect the petiole/rachis for a small raised gland just above the leaf base.
2 · Count PAIRS of primary pinnae on the whole leaf, then the much smaller paired leaflets on each pinna.
3 · Seek an undisturbed flowering head, count flowers and (with hand lens) stamens per bisexual flower; do NOT equate long white stamens to petals.
4 · Examine several mature pods WITH SCALE. Record pod length, WIDTH and whether strongly sickle-shaped versus almost straight.
5 · Check branching posture and fine stem/leaf hair; treat these as supporting traits only.
6 · If only leaves are available, teach genus identification and leave species uncertain rather than guessing from foliage alone.

comparison_matrix.acuminatus: 4–6 pairs (UT Austin Williamson flora; count all pinnae on full leaf)

comparison_matrix.virgatus: Small whitish heads; numerical ranges variable

field_quick_key.look: Pods conspicuously wide (4.5–7 mm), short (15–32 mm), strongly sickle-curved and crowded
Pods narrow (2–3 mm), long (35–70 mm), nearly straight; heads often only 4–12 flowers; fine leaflets
3–7 pairs of pinnae, stems fine-velvety, heads roughly 15–33 flowers, 10 stamens
Spreading stems, 4–6 pairs of pinnae, often 6–16-flowered heads, 10 stamens, and pointed pods about 30–50 mm; confirm against virgatus before precise ID
Variable thin-podded plants that do not clearly fit foregoing; historically broad taxon concept
field_quick_key.likely: Desmanthus virgatus, provisional pending full stem + pod + flower review

lookalikes.look: Desmanthus typically unarmed with gland on petiole/rachis near proximal pinnae; Mimosa can be prickly with different leaflet/gland and flower structure; leaf folding not exclusive
Similar bipinnate leaves and flower puff; inspect petiolar glands and detailed head/flower structure; Neptunia often yellow and its leaf head structure differs
Leucaena develops woody tree/shrub stems and long clusters of seedpods; genus-level flower and leaf comparisons needed
Often pinnate leaf rather than bipinnate, with bright yellow irregular flowers rather than little white pompom heads
Can be woody, armed/prickly or have distinctive thorn pairs; look at entire leaf and axillary spines before calling herbaceous bundleflower

scientific_guardrails: Source-pool admission is NOT strict target-county native PASS. Preserve UNRESOLVED until 3 county evidence independently assessed.
D. acuminatus is accepted separately from D. virgatus by ITIS/POWO; D. virgatus var. acuminatus is a historical synonym of acuminatus, not a second learner card.
One image of a flowering puffball cannot separate most Desmanthus species; true seedpod shape and count are required.
Photographs from botanical gardens, overseas naturalizations, and cultivation cannot serve as native Texas county evidence.
D. leptolobus and D. acuminatus image rights are not yet secure from current first-pass candidates; never use an image of another taxon as a substitute.
Some records labelled D. virgatus may be broad species-complex or forage cultivars; identify local Texas plants by specimen concept.
diagnostic_photo_checklist: Same-scale whole leaves with pinnae and leaflet counts, plus gland at basal rachis
Macro of single flower head with flower count and 5-vs-10 stamens
Close-up of mature pods of each species with millimeter ruler showing shape and width
Macro of velvet hair on D. velutinus stem
Noncultivated Central Texas evidence for D. acuminatus and D. leptolobus
Side-by-side D. acuminatus vs D. virgatus using fruits and mature foliage
Arrow annotations ONLY after verified on actual installed JPEGs

visual_comparison.title: Bundleflowers: the pods tell the story
visual_comparison.subtitle: Photo-first genus guide: 12 physically installed exact-species JPEGs; seven individually checked structure examples and two explicitly missing macro views. Five source-pool species are covered. Arrows await precise point-by-point image review.
visual_comparison.memory_rule: First count PINNAE and LEAFLETS; then compare POD SHAPE. Illinois = short/broad/crescent; prairie = long/thin/nearly straight. Flower heads consist of many tiny flowers, not one puffball flower.

part_examples.title: Count pinnae and leaflets
part_examples.look_for: Start where the whole leaf meets the stem. Pinnae are the larger featherlike branches; leaflets are the small paired blades on them. The installed image shows this overall pattern, but not a close gland.
part_examples.why_it_matters: Distinguishes the leaf construction from a merely pinnate legume leaf and teaches how to count pinnae across bundleflowers.

part_examples.title: Find the puffball flower head
part_examples.look_for: Find the spherical cluster of many tiny whitish flowers with projecting white filaments. This modest-resolution image shows the head shape; it does not permit an accurate 10-stamen count.
part_examples.why_it_matters: Desmanthus has many tiny flowers together; do not confuse the entire head with a single large flower.

part_examples.title: See a developing pod bundle
part_examples.look_for: At the center of the photograph, green curved pods develop in a bundle. Several compound leaves and small flower heads are also visible.
part_examples.why_it_matters: Shows how the conspicuous fruit cluster is attached to the head-bearing stalk.

part_examples.title: Compare the broad sickle pods
part_examples.look_for: Mature pods curl into a compact brown cluster, with distinct seed outlines and opened pod walls.
part_examples.why_it_matters: Short, wider, strongly curved pods are one of the best characters distinguishing Illinois bundleflower.

part_examples.title: Compare long, slender pods
part_examples.look_for: Two long, very narrow brown pods lie across a hand. These are from a Texas prairie bundleflower observation, NOT Illinois bundleflower.
part_examples.why_it_matters: The thin, straighter pods make the difference much easier to remember than leaf color or height.

part_examples.title: Look at pointed pods and seeds
part_examples.look_for: Several narrow, sharp-tipped pods and loose small dark seeds lie on a hand; the photo has an original identification label from its source.
part_examples.why_it_matters: Connects sharp-pod bundleflower's name with a real fruit structure and demonstrates that each pod holds seeds.

part_examples.title: See what a mature seed looks like
part_examples.look_for: Five brown seeds isolated against blue, with a 2-mm scale. The visible mark on the seed surface is part of the seed coat, not a leaflet or petal.
part_examples.why_it_matters: Links the pod cluster to the small individual seeds it contains.

part_examples.title: Find the tiny leaf-base gland
part_examples.look_for: With a 10× lens, inspect the upper petiole/rachis beside the LOWEST pinnae for a little raised nectary. Do not point to the pulvini or leaflets by mistake.
part_examples.why_it_matters: Useful when a plant resembles Mimosa or Neptunia, but we still need one exact-species in-focus gland photograph.

part_examples.title: Count stamens in one flower
part_examples.look_for: Photograph ONE open bisexual flower from above at macro scale and count the free stamens, rather than trying to count the entire puffball head.
part_examples.why_it_matters: Five versus ten stamens helps separate D. illinoensis/leptolobus from D. acuminatus/velutinus; the current whole-head photos are not sharp enough.

genus_diagnostics.leaves: Whole twice-compound (bipinnate) leaf: count pinnae (the featherlike side branches) and leaflets (the tiny paired blades attached to each pinna). In the installed D. acuminatus photo several complete leaves are plainly visible.
genus_diagnostics.inflorescence: Small roughly spherical flower HEAD made up of many separate tiny flowers. The white brushy look is mostly stamens, not five large petals. Installed velvet bundleflower photo shows the whole flowering head but not every separate stamen.
genus_diagnostics.fruit: Flat individual legume PODS form a clustered bundle. The mature short, broad, strongly sickle-shaped pods of D. illinoensis differ strikingly from the long narrow nearly straight pods of D. leptolobus.
genus_diagnostics.stem: Leaf-base Gland (extrafloral nectary): a tiny raised spot on the upper petiole/rachis between the lowest pinnae. This is a real character but the present photos do NOT show it sharply enough for a confident arrow.
genus_diagnostics.habit: Generally unarmed perennial herbs to low subshrubs with feathery leaves. Height and whether stems spread or stand upright vary; confirm species with flower and mature pods instead.
